Overall Product Character
These men's brown denim jeans are made in Japan by Studio D'Artisan and combine the construction of classic five-pocket jeans with two distinctive Japanese production techniques: low-speed denim weaving on a Toyoda GL-3 power loom and traditional Amami Dorozome mud dyeing.

The jeans are constructed from substantial 15 oz. cotton denim woven from undyed ecru warp and weft yarns. After the denim is cut and sewn into jeans, the completed garment is dyed on Amami Oshima using a repeated botanical-dyeing and mud-treatment process. This creates a deep, earthy brown color with natural variations in tone.

The irregular surface of the GL-3-woven denim contains visible neps, uneven yarn thickness, fine raised cotton fibers that create a subtly fuzzy surface, and irregular variations in texture. These characteristics are combined with the naturally developed brown coloration of Amami Dorozome to create a fabric that differs in both appearance and feel from conventional indigo denim.

The design follows the traditional structure of five-pocket jeans, including a button fly, curved front hand pockets, a coin pocket, rear patch pockets, metal rivets, five belt loops, and a leather brand patch. The result is a practical pair of everyday jeans with a distinctive fabric texture and naturally developed brown color.

Silhouette and Fit
These jeans have a classic regular straight fit with a standard mid rise. The silhouette is neither excessively loose nor closely tapered.

The upper legs provide moderate room through the thighs, allowing comfortable movement without creating an oversized appearance. From the knees to the leg openings, the legs narrow very slightly while maintaining the natural line of traditional straight-leg jeans.

The balanced proportions preserve the substantial appearance associated with classic workwear while remaining easy to coordinate with contemporary casual clothing. The regular straight shape can be worn with boots, sneakers, or other everyday footwear without appearing strongly influenced by short-term fashion trends.

15 oz. GL-3 Loom-Woven Denim
The jeans are made from 15 oz. denim woven from 100% cotton yarn on a Toyoda GL-3 power loom. The GL-3 was manufactured by Toyoda Automatic Loom Works, now known as Toyota Industries Corporation, during the 1950s and is considered one of Japan's early motorized power looms.

Unlike modern high-speed textile machinery, the GL-3 operates at an extremely low production rate. It can weave only approximately five meters of fabric per hour. This slow weaving speed allows the yarns to retain more of their natural irregularity and prevents the fabric from becoming excessively compressed, flat, or mechanically uniform.

The resulting denim has a substantial hand and a visibly irregular surface. Variations in yarn thickness and placement create neps, rough areas, uneven elevations, and fine raised cotton fibers that give the fabric a slightly fuzzy surface appearance.

The combination of surface fuzz, neps, irregular yarn thickness, and rough texture gives the denim a dry, rugged, and three-dimensional character that is different from the smooth and uniform surface of conventionally manufactured denim.

These characteristics are not manufacturing defects. They are inherent features of denim produced from irregular yarns on early low-speed weaving equipment.

Studio D'Artisan Original Denim Specification
The denim was developed according to Studio D'Artisan's original fabric specification. The yarn count, yarn shape, warp and weft density, number of inserted yarns, and weaving conditions were selected to emphasize the distinctive characteristics of the GL-3 loom.

The interaction between the irregular cotton yarns and the low-speed weaving process produces a surface that is not uniformly smooth. Small neps, uneven yarn thickness, fine raised cotton fibers, and irregular variations in texture may be visible throughout the garment.

The fine cotton fibers extending from the surface create a subtle degree of fuzziness. This surface character is a natural result of the yarn and weaving specifications and should not be confused with pilling or fabric damage.

The substantial 15 oz. weight gives the jeans a firm structure, while the irregular texture and fine surface fuzz create a three-dimensional appearance that becomes more noticeable under changing light and through continued wear.

Undyed Ecru Warp and Weft Yarns
Both the warp and weft yarns are initially undyed ecru cotton. This differs from conventional blue denim, which is normally woven with indigo-dyed warp yarns and undyed weft yarns.

These jeans are not made by taking conventional indigo denim and redyeing it brown. Instead, the GL-3 denim is woven entirely from undyed yarns before the completed garment is treated with Amami Dorozome mud dyeing.

Beginning with an undyed denim base allows the natural dye to penetrate both the warp and weft yarns. This produces a brown color throughout the structure of the cloth while preserving the neps, fine surface fuzz, uneven elevations, and rough texture created during weaving.

Amami Dorozome Mud-Dyeing Process
The jeans are dyed using Amami Dorozome, a traditional natural dyeing method practiced on Amami Oshima, an island in southern Japan.

The process uses a botanical dye extracted from the locally grown Techi tree, known in Japanese as Sharinbai. Its botanical classification is Rhaphiolepis indica var. umbellata. The wood and bark of the tree contain natural tannins that can penetrate cotton fibers and react with iron.

The garment is repeatedly immersed in the plant-based dye solution so that the tannins can gradually enter the cotton fibers. It is then immersed in iron-rich mud from Amami Oshima.

The iron contained in the mud reacts with the tannins absorbed into the fabric. This natural chemical reaction darkens the material and helps fix the color within the cotton fibers. Repeated botanical-dyeing and mud-treatment cycles gradually build the deep, earthy brown tone.

The process requires considerable time and repeated manual work. Because the final color is created through the interaction of plant-derived tannins, iron-rich mud, water, cotton yarn, and individual processing conditions, the resulting shade is not mechanically uniform.

Minor differences in color depth, surface tone, and dye concentration may occur between individual pairs and between different areas of the same garment. These variations are inherent characteristics of traditional natural dyeing and should not be regarded as defects.

Garment-Dyed Construction
The jeans are dyed after the denim has been cut and sewn into a completed garment. This garment-dyeing method allows the Amami Dorozome color to develop across the main fabric, seams, pocket edges, belt loops, reinforced areas, and other structural details.

Because areas containing multiple layers of denim may absorb and retain the dye differently from single-layer areas, subtle tonal differences may appear around the seams, pockets, waistband, fly, and hems.

The neps, raised cotton fibers, rough areas, and uneven elevations of the GL-3 denim may also absorb and reflect the color differently. This interaction between the irregular fabric surface and the natural dye contributes to the depth and variation of the finished brown color.

These small differences contribute to the natural appearance of the finished jeans and reflect the interaction between the garment's construction, the GL-3-woven denim, and the traditional dyeing process.

One-Wash Finish
The finished jeans have been washed once before sale. This one-wash treatment removes a portion of the initial shrinkage and softens the rigid feel of newly woven 15 oz. denim, allowing the jeans to feel more comfortable and easier to wear from the beginning.

Although the one-wash process reduces initial shrinkage, minor additional shrinkage or dimensional change may still occur depending on water temperature, washing method, drying conditions, and frequency of laundering.

The fabric may also stretch slightly in areas exposed to repeated movement and pressure, particularly around the waist, seat, knees, and thighs. This combination of minor shrinkage and wear-related stretching is a normal characteristic of cotton denim.

Wear and Color Development
The mud-dyed brown surface will gradually change through repeated wear, friction, movement, and washing. Areas exposed to frequent abrasion, including the pocket openings, fly edges, knees, thighs, seams, hems, and rear pocket edges, may gradually develop lighter tones and more visible surface contrast.

The fine raised fibers on the surface may gradually settle, flatten, or wear away in areas exposed to repeated friction. At the same time, recessed sections may retain more of their original fuzziness and darker color. This difference can make the irregular elevations, neps, and three-dimensional texture of the GL-3 denim increasingly visible.

The resulting color and texture development will vary according to the wearer's body shape, movement, frequency of wear, washing method, drying conditions, and daily use. No two pairs will develop exactly the same appearance.

Because natural dyeing does not produce the same perfectly uniform and highly colorfast surface associated with some modern synthetic dye systems, gradual fading, tonal variation, and occasional color transfer should be regarded as inherent characteristics of the jeans.

Five-Button Button Fly
The front opening uses a traditional button-fly construction. It consists of one top button at the waistband and four buttons along the fly, for a total of five buttons.

The buttons are made from metal and finished with a black coating that coordinates with the earthy brown denim. Each button is stamped with the Studio D'Artisan brand logo.

The button fly reinforces the classic five-pocket construction and provides a more traditional appearance than a zipper fly. With extended use, friction may gradually alter the black coating on the raised edges of the buttons. This surface change is a natural result of wear.

Curved Front Hand Pockets
Curved hand pockets are positioned on the left and right sides of the front body. The openings are shaped to provide practical access while maintaining the familiar appearance of classic five-pocket jeans.

Metal rivets reinforce the ends of the pocket openings. These areas receive concentrated stress when the wearer inserts a hand or carries an object inside the pocket. The rivets help distribute this stress and reduce the possibility of the pocket corners separating from the surrounding denim.

The pocket openings and riveted corners may gradually develop lighter color and more pronounced surface contrast through repeated use.

Coin Pocket
A coin pocket is incorporated into the right front pocket area. It follows the compact construction traditionally used on classic five-pocket jeans.

The coin pocket is also reinforced with metal rivets at stress points. Although originally intended for carrying small items, it also serves as a recognizable structural and visual detail associated with traditional jeans.

Rear Patch Pockets and Hidden Rivets
Two patch pockets are positioned on the back, one on each side. They are constructed from the same 15 oz. Amami Dorozome mud-dyed denim as the main body.

The upper corners of the rear pockets are reinforced with hidden rivets installed inside the pocket construction. These rivets strengthen the high-stress attachment points while remaining concealed from the exterior.

This construction preserves a clean outer appearance while providing reinforcement similar to the exposed rivets used on the front pockets.

Signature Back-Pocket Stitching
Both rear pockets feature Studio D'Artisan's original decorative stitching pattern. The stitching is applied in a brown-toned thread selected to coordinate with the mud-dyed fabric.

The restrained color reduces strong contrast and allows the stitching to remain integrated with the overall earthy appearance of the jeans.

As the surrounding denim changes through wear and washing, the relationship between the pocket stitching and the fabric color may gradually become more visible.

Five Belt Loops
The waistband is equipped with five belt loops positioned around the waist. This traditional arrangement provides practical support for a belt while maintaining the balanced construction of classic five-pocket jeans.

The belt loops are made from the same mud-dyed denim. Their raised edges and areas of contact with a belt may develop lighter color and surface wear over time.

Leather Brand Patch
A Studio D'Artisan leather brand patch is sewn onto the right rear section of the waistband. The patch identifies the brand while adding a natural material that will change through continued wear.

The leather may gradually soften and develop changes in color and surface texture through exposure to friction, moisture, body heat, and daily use.

Natural differences in grain, tone, and texture may be visible in the leather. These variations are inherent characteristics of the material rather than defects.

Classic Five-Pocket Construction
The jeans follow the basic structure of traditional five-pocket workwear, including two curved front hand pockets, one coin pocket, two rear patch pockets, riveted stress points, a button fly, five belt loops, and a rear leather patch.

Rather than serving as a reproduction of one specific historical model, the design combines these established jeans details with Studio D'Artisan's original 15 oz. GL-3 denim and the natural coloration of Amami Dorozome mud dyeing.

The result is a regular straight pair of jeans that retains the practical structure of traditional workwear while presenting a naturally developed brown color, fine surface fuzz, and irregular texture created through specialized Japanese weaving and dyeing processes.

Natural-Dye Color Transfer
These jeans are colored with natural dye. Excess dye remaining on or near the fabric surface may transfer to other materials through friction.

Particular care should be taken during the initial period of wear. Avoid combining the jeans with white or light-colored clothing, bags, shoes, belts, furniture, automobile seats, upholstery, or other items that may easily absorb pigment.

Color transfer may occur while the jeans are dry, but the risk increases when the fabric is damp from perspiration, rain, washing, or high humidity. Areas exposed to repeated friction may also release color more readily.

Do not place the wet or damp jeans directly against other clothing or household surfaces. Do not leave the garment folded, compressed, or in contact with another item while wet, as dissolved dye may migrate and create staining.

Washing and Care Precautions
Wash these jeans separately from other garments because released dye may transfer during washing.

Turn the jeans inside out before washing to reduce direct abrasion against the dyed outer surface. Use cold or lukewarm water, a mild detergent, and a gentle washing cycle. Avoid excessive agitation, scrubbing, brushing, or concentrated rubbing.

Do not use chlorine bleach or oxygen bleach. Avoid hot water and tumble drying. Do not leave the jeans soaking for an extended period, as prolonged immersion may cause excessive dye loss or uneven color migration.

After washing, remove the jeans promptly, reshape them carefully, and allow them to air-dry naturally in the shade. Do not leave the garment wet or folded for an extended period.

Because of the natural dyeing process, some color loss is expected during washing. Variations in fading and surface tone are part of the intended character of the garment.

Always follow the specific care instructions attached to the product.

Made in Japan
These jeans are made in Japan from Studio D'Artisan's original 15 oz. cotton denim woven on a Toyoda GL-3 power loom and colored using traditional Amami Dorozome mud dyeing.

The irregular fabric surface, fine cotton fuzz, natural coloration, hardware, five-pocket construction, and regular straight silhouette combine specialized Japanese textile production with the practical design principles of classic jeans.


Toyoda GL-3 Power Loom

An Early Japanese Power Loom
The GL-3 is an early Japanese shuttle-type power loom manufactured by Toyoda Automatic Loom Works, now known as Toyota Industries Corporation. It was produced during the 1950s and represents an early stage in the development of motorized weaving technology in Japan.

Only a limited number of GL-3 looms were manufactured, and very few remain operational today. Their rarity, low production capacity, and distinctive weaving characteristics have made them highly valued for producing specialized fabrics with pronounced surface variation.

Difficult to Maintain
Replacement parts for the GL-3 are no longer commercially manufactured. When a component becomes worn or damaged, usable parts may need to be recovered from another retired or non-operational GL-3 loom.

Keeping the machine in working condition requires experienced technicians who understand its mechanical timing, shuttle movement, yarn tension, take-up system, and other operating characteristics.

Small changes in alignment or mechanical adjustment can affect both the stability of the weaving process and the appearance of the finished fabric. Regular inspection, careful adjustment, and continued maintenance are therefore essential.

Extremely Slow Weaving Speed
A GL-3 can weave only approximately five meters of fabric per hour. This is considerably slower than contemporary high-speed looms designed for large-scale industrial production.

From a manufacturing perspective, the GL-3 is highly inefficient. It requires more time, closer supervision, and greater mechanical attention to produce a relatively small quantity of fabric.

However, the slow operating speed allows the yarns to be woven without creating the highly compressed, smooth, and mechanically uniform surface commonly associated with modern mass-produced textiles.

Why the GL-3 Is Called a "Phantom Loom"
The GL-3 is sometimes referred to as a "phantom loom" because very few operational machines remain, replacement parts are difficult to obtain, and the technical knowledge required to maintain them is increasingly specialized.

The term also refers to the distinctive fabric character produced by the machine. Depending on the yarn and weaving specifications, the GL-3 can produce visible neps, slubs, uneven elevations, fine surface fuzz, and subtle variations in surface density that are difficult to reproduce with modern high-speed equipment.

These characteristics are not manufacturing defects. They result from the combination of irregular yarns, low-speed weaving, carefully controlled tension, and the mechanical properties of the older loom.

Fabric Characteristics Produced by the GL-3
Fabric woven on the GL-3 typically has a substantial hand and a visibly irregular surface. Differences in yarn thickness, tension, and placement create raised and recessed areas throughout the cloth.

Small neps, slubs, fine raised cotton fibers, and irregular variations in texture may be visible. Neps are small groups of entangled fibers, while slubs are thicker sections formed within intentionally irregular yarns.

The fine cotton fibers extending from the surface give the fabric a subtly fuzzy appearance and tactile texture. This natural surface fuzz is distinct from pilling and is an intended characteristic of the denim.

Rather than appearing perfectly flat and uniform, the surface contains subtle variations that become more noticeable under changing light and through continued use.

The exact appearance and hand of the fabric depend on the yarn count, yarn irregularity, warp density, weft density, weaving tension, and other production specifications selected for each fabric.

Craftsmanship Rather Than Production Efficiency
Producing fabric on the GL-3 requires substantially more time and manual involvement than weaving on modern industrial machinery.

The loom must be carefully maintained, weaving conditions must be monitored, and mechanical adjustments may be required during production. The objective is not maximum output or complete visual uniformity, but the creation of fabric with controlled irregularity and distinctive surface character.

Each length of fabric reflects the interaction between the loom, the yarn specification, the mechanical settings, and the judgment of the loom operator.

The GL-3 therefore represents a production method that prioritizes fabric character, technical skill, and careful small-scale manufacturing over speed and efficiency.

Handling Amami Dorozome Mud-Dyed Products

Traditional Amami Dorozome Dyeing
Amami Dorozome is a traditional mud-dyeing method practiced on Amami Oshima in southern Japan.

The process uses a botanical dye extracted from the Techi tree, also known in Japanese as Sharinbai. The wood and bark contain natural tannins that can bond with textile fibers and react with iron.

The material is repeatedly immersed in the plant-based dye solution so that the tannins penetrate the fibers. It is then treated with iron-rich mud from Amami Oshima.

The iron in the mud reacts with the tannins and gradually deepens and fixes the color. Multiple dyeing and mud-treatment cycles are required to build the characteristic earthy tone.

Natural Color Variation
Amami Dorozome does not produce the mechanically uniform appearance associated with conventional synthetic dyeing.

Minor differences in color depth, concentration, and surface tone may occur between individual products. Subtle variations may also be visible within different areas of the same product.

Seams, folds, reinforced areas, and sections containing multiple layers of fabric may absorb or retain the dye differently from single-layer areas.

These variations are inherent characteristics of the traditional dyeing process and should not be regarded as defects.

Color Transfer Through Friction
Natural dye remaining on or near the surface may transfer to other materials through friction.

Particular care should be taken when a mud-dyed product comes into contact with white or light-colored clothing, bags, shoes, furniture, automobile seats, upholstery, or other finished surfaces.

Areas exposed to repeated rubbing may release color more readily. Color transfer is often more noticeable during the early period of use, although it may continue depending on moisture, friction, and washing conditions.

Color Transfer When Wet or Damp
Moisture can increase the possibility of dye transfer. Perspiration, rain, washing water, humidity, or other sources of moisture may cause the surface dye to become more mobile.

When the product is damp, avoid direct contact with light-colored clothing, bags, furniture, automobile seats, and other materials that may absorb the dye.

Do not leave the wet product folded, compressed, or placed against another item for an extended period. Prolonged contact while wet may result in color transfer, uneven staining, or migration of dye between different sections.

Washing Instructions
Wash mud-dyed products separately from other items because released dye may transfer during washing.

When appropriate for the product, turn it inside out before washing. This reduces direct abrasion against the dyed outer surface and may help limit unnecessary surface color loss.

Use cold or lukewarm water, a mild detergent, and a gentle washing method. Avoid excessive mechanical agitation, scrubbing, brushing, or concentrated rubbing.

Do not use chlorine bleach or oxygen bleach. Avoid hot water and tumble drying unless specifically permitted by the care label attached to the product.

After washing, remove the product promptly, reshape it carefully, and allow it to air-dry naturally in the shade. Do not leave it soaking or wet for an extended period.

Always follow the specific care instructions provided on the product label.

Drying and Sunlight Precautions
When appropriate, turn the product inside out before drying and place it in a well-ventilated shaded area.

Avoid prolonged exposure to direct sunlight. Strong ultraviolet light may cause natural dyes to fade, discolor, or change unevenly, particularly when the product remains exposed in the same position for an extended period.

Direct sunlight should not be used intentionally to darken or develop the color, as it may instead cause unwanted or uneven fading.

Natural Aging and Color Development
The color and surface appearance of Amami Dorozome products will gradually change through use, friction, washing, moisture, and exposure to air.

Areas that receive frequent contact may become lighter, while recessed or less exposed areas may retain a darker tone. The resulting appearance will vary according to how the product is used, cleaned, dried, and stored.

No two naturally dyed products will develop in exactly the same manner.

Characteristics of Natural Dye
Color fading, surface variation, and occasional color transfer are inherent characteristics of Amami Dorozome and other natural dyeing methods.

These properties differ from the high degree of color uniformity and colorfastness commonly associated with modern synthetic dyes.

Careful handling can reduce unwanted transfer and uneven fading, but it cannot completely prevent the natural color from changing over time.

Please handle Amami Dorozome products with appropriate care and enjoy the individual color development and surface character created through continued use.

Care Instructions
Machine wash on a gentle cycle at a maximum water temperature of 40°C (104°F).
Do not use chlorine bleach or oxygen bleach.
Iron at a medium temperature with a pressing cloth placed between the iron and the garment.
Do not dry clean.
Due to the nature of the dye, color loss may occur. Wash separately from other garments.
Due to the characteristics of the fabric, slight shrinkage may occur after washing.
Color may transfer to other clothing, accessories, upholstery, or other surfaces through friction or when the garment is damp from perspiration, rain, or other moisture.

This men's brown denim jacket is made in Japan by Studio D'Artisan (SDA) and combines a classic workwear-inspired design with two distinctive Japanese production methods. The 15 oz. denim is woven from undyed ecru warp and weft yarns on a vintage GL-3 loom manufactured by Toyoda Automatic Loom Works, now known as Toyota Industries Corporation. This process produces an earthy brown tone with subtle variations from piece to piece. Overall Product Character
This men's brown denim jacket is made in Japan by Studio D'Artisan and combines the construction of a classic early work jacket with two distinctive Japanese production techniques: low-speed denim weaving on a Toyoda GL-3 power loom and traditional Amami Dorozome mud dyeing. The jacket is constructed from substantial 15 oz. cotton denim woven from undyed ecru warp and weft yarns. After construction, the garment is dyed to create its earthy brown color.

The design is characterized by a short body length, vertically arranged front pleats, lower patch pockets, action pleats across the back, and an adjustable cinch-back strap. These functional details are derived from early workwear construction, but Studio D'Artisan has modified the overall balance and fabric specification to create a jacket suitable for contemporary casual wear.

This is an unlined, single-layer jacket. It can be worn as a light outer layer during spring and fall, over a T-shirt or lightweight shirt in milder weather, or as an intermediate layer under a heavier coat during colder seasons.

Silhouette and Fit
The jacket has a classic work-jacket silhouette with moderate room through the chest and torso, a relatively short body length, and a straight shape from the chest to the hem. It is not cut closely to follow the contours of the body, but it is also not designed with the substantially dropped shoulders or exaggerated proportions associated with modern oversized clothing.

The shoulder width is kept relatively natural, allowing the set-in sleeves to follow the wearer's shoulder line without creating excessive volume. The chest and body provide practical ease of movement, while the short length allows the hem to sit around the waist or upper hip area, depending on the wearer's height and body proportions.

The sleeves are designed with a standard length and a conventional set-in construction. The overall fit reflects the proportions of a vintage work jacket, providing enough room for layering while maintaining a controlled and balanced appearance.

15 oz. GL-3 Loom-Woven Denim
The jacket is made from 15 oz. denim woven from 100% cotton yarn on a Toyoda GL-3 power loom. The GL-3 was one of the earliest power looms developed in Japan and represents an important stage in the development of the Japanese textile industry.

Unlike modern high-speed weaving equipment, the GL-3 operates at an extremely low production rate. It is capable of weaving only approximately five meters of fabric per hour. This slow weaving speed allows the yarns to retain more of their natural irregularity and prevents the fabric from becoming excessively compressed or mechanically uniform.

Replacement components for the GL-3 are no longer commercially produced. Maintaining an operational loom may require usable parts to be recovered from other retired GL-3 machines. The limited availability of replacement parts, specialized mechanical adjustment, and low production efficiency make the continued use of this loom exceptionally labor-intensive.

The resulting denim has a firm, substantial hand with visible surface irregularity. Natural yarn thickness variation produces small neps, raised fibers, and uneven areas across the fabric. These characteristics are not manufacturing defects. They are inherent features of denim produced on early low-speed weaving equipment.

Studio D'Artisan Original Denim Specification
The denim was developed according to Studio D'Artisan's original fabric specification. The yarn count, yarn irregularity, warp and weft density, and weaving tension were selected to emphasize the distinctive characteristics of the GL-3 loom.

Both the warp and weft yarns are initially undyed ecru cotton. This differs from conventional blue denim, which is normally woven with indigo-dyed warp yarns and undyed weft yarns. By beginning with an entirely ecru denim base, the finished fabric can absorb the Amami Dorozome dye across both sets of yarns, producing a brown color that extends throughout the structure of the cloth.

The combination of irregular yarns, low-speed weaving, and substantial 15 oz. weight gives the fabric a pronounced three-dimensional surface. The cloth is not uniformly smooth. Instead, it contains subtle changes in yarn thickness, tension, and elevation that become more visible as the jacket is worn and washed.

Amami Dorozome Mud-Dyeing Process
The jacket is dyed using Amami Dorozome, a traditional dyeing technique practiced on Amami Oshima, an island in southern Japan. The process uses dye extracted from the locally grown Techi tree, also known as Sharinbai in Japanese. Its botanical classification is Rhaphiolepis indica var. umbellata.

The wood and bark of the Techi tree contain natural tannins. These materials are processed to create a botanical dye bath, and the garment is repeatedly immersed in the solution so that the tannins can penetrate the cotton fibers. The garment is then treated with the iron-rich mud found on Amami Oshima.

The iron in the mud reacts with the tannins absorbed into the fabric. This natural chemical reaction darkens the material and helps fix the color within the cotton fibers. Repeated botanical-dye and mud-treatment cycles gradually build the final earthy brown tone.

Because the coloration is created through repeated interaction between plant-derived tannins, iron-rich mud, water, cotton yarn, and manual processing, the resulting shade is not mechanically uniform. Minor variations in depth, surface tone, and color concentration may occur between individual garments and between different areas of the same garment. These variations are characteristic of the traditional dyeing method.

The finished color has a natural soil-like depth that differs from the flatter and more uniform appearance commonly produced by conventional synthetic dyes. The brown tone also emphasizes the neps, raised fibers, and irregular texture of the GL-3-woven denim.

One-Wash Finish
The finished jacket has been washed once before sale. This one-wash treatment removes a portion of the initial shrinkage and softens the rigid feel of newly woven denim, allowing the jacket to feel more comfortable and easier to wear from the beginning.

Although the one-wash process stabilizes the fabric to a certain degree, minor additional shrinkage or dimensional change may still occur depending on water temperature, washing method, drying conditions, and frequency of laundering. Cold water and natural air drying are recommended to reduce unnecessary shrinkage and color loss.

Wear and Color Development
The mud-dyed surface will gradually change through repeated wear, friction, movement, and washing. Areas exposed to frequent contact, including the seams, front pleats, pocket openings, cuffs, elbows, collar edges, and waistband, may develop lighter tones and more pronounced surface contrast.

The raised portions of the irregular denim surface will generally receive more abrasion than the recessed areas. This difference in friction can emphasize the fabric's uneven texture over time. The resulting color variation will depend on how the jacket is worn, how frequently it is washed, and the conditions in which it is used.

Because natural dyeing does not produce the same perfectly uniform and highly colorfast surface as some modern synthetic dye systems, gradual color transfer and fading should be regarded as inherent characteristics of the garment.

Collar Construction
The jacket has a simple shirt-style collar without a separate collar stand. The collar is attached directly to the neckline rather than being mounted on a raised band.

This construction keeps the collar base relatively low and creates a flatter roll than a collar with a separate stand. The result is a compact neckline that is consistent with the direct and functional construction of early work jackets.

Five-Button Front Closure
The front closes with five metal buttons positioned vertically along the front opening. The buttonholes are sewn horizontally, a traditional orientation that helps the button remain seated against lateral pulling forces generated when the wearer moves the arms or expands the chest.

The front placket is formed by folding the denim back on itself to create a double-layer structure. This reinforces the button and buttonhole area, helps control stretching along the front opening, and provides additional resistance to distortion during repeated fastening and unfastening.

Vertical Front Pleats
Four vertical front pleats are incorporated into the front body, with two pleats positioned on each side of the front opening. The pleats run parallel to the button placket, extending from below the front yoke to the upper edge of the waistband.

Each pleat is formed by folding a section of the front-body fabric inward and securing the fold at three separate points with horizontal rows of stitching. This construction retains a controlled amount of additional fabric within each front panel.

When the wearer reaches forward, raises the arms, or expands the chest, the folded sections can open slightly to provide additional ease across the chest and front body. This helps compensate for the limited stretch of the substantial 15 oz. denim and reduces pulling around the button placket, armholes, and upper front panels.

When the wearer returns to a neutral position, the pleats settle back into their folded configuration. This allows the front body to maintain a relatively flat and controlled appearance without the permanent fullness that would result from a wider body pattern.

In addition to their functional purpose, the four pleats create pronounced vertical lines extending along both sides of the front opening. This construction emphasizes the elongated panel structure and distinctive appearance associated with early work-jacket design.

Lower Patch Pockets
Two patch pockets are positioned on the lower front body, one on each side. The pockets have an open-top design without flaps, providing direct access while maintaining a simple and functional appearance.

The upper corners of each pocket are reinforced with metal rivets. These locations receive concentrated stress when the wearer inserts a hand or carries an object inside the pocket. The rivets help distribute this load and reduce the possibility of the pocket corners separating from the body fabric.

The pockets are constructed from the same 15 oz. mud-dyed denim as the main body. As the jacket is worn, the pocket edges and riveted corners may develop visible abrasion and color contrast.

Set-In Sleeve Construction
The sleeves are attached to the body with conventional set-in armholes. Unlike a dropped-shoulder or raglan construction, the sleeve seam is positioned close to the natural shoulder point.

This construction gives the shoulder area a controlled shape and allows the sleeve to extend naturally from the upper body. It also helps preserve the structured appearance associated with classic work jackets.

Button Cuffs and Riveted Cuff Slits
Each sleeve is finished with a single-button cuff. A cuff slit is positioned above the cuff opening to provide enough space for the hand to pass through the sleeve and to allow the cuff to open during dressing.

A reinforcing metal rivet is installed at the upper end of each cuff slit. This point is exposed to repeated pulling and concentrated stress when the cuff is opened, closed, or pulled over the hand. The rivet helps reduce the risk of the slit extending or tearing into the sleeve fabric.

Black-Coated Metal Buttons
The front and cuff buttons are made from metal and finished with a black coating. Each button is stamped with the Studio D'Artisan brand logo.

The dark hardware coordinates with the earthy brown denim while maintaining a restrained industrial appearance. With extended wear, friction may gradually alter the surface of the black coating, particularly along raised edges and areas that frequently contact the buttonholes.

Straight Back Yoke
The upper back is divided by a straight horizontal yoke extending across the shoulders. This yoke supports the upper portion of the jacket and provides a stable structural transition between the shoulder area and the lower back panels.

Below the yoke, the back body is constructed from two panels joined by a vertical center seam. The center seam helps shape and stabilize the wide back area while maintaining the symmetrical appearance of the jacket.

Rear Action Pleats
Vertical action pleats are positioned on both sides of the back body. The pleats extend from below the back yoke toward the waistband area.

When the wearer reaches forward, lifts the arms, or moves the shoulders, these pleats can open to release additional fabric across the upper back. This increases mobility through the shoulder blades and reduces the amount of pulling transferred directly to the armholes, shoulder seams, and back yoke.

When the arms return to a neutral position, the pleats fold back toward the body. This allows the jacket to provide additional movement without requiring a permanently wide or oversized back silhouette.

Adjustable Cinch-Back Strap
An adjustable cinch-back strap is positioned near the lower back. The two ends of the strap are secured to the body with metal rivets, and the strap passes through a metal buckle.

Tightening the buckle draws in a portion of the fabric at the rear waistband, allowing the wearer to make a limited adjustment to the circumference and shape of the lower back. Loosening the strap restores more room through the hem.

The cinch-back is both a functional adjustment device and a characteristic detail associated with early workwear construction.

Please note that the exposed buckle and rivets may scratch or abrade surfaces such as automobile seats, leather or fabric sofas, chairs, painted furniture, and other finished materials. Care should be taken when sitting or leaning against delicate surfaces.

Leather Brand Patch
A Studio D'Artisan leather brand patch is attached inside the jacket at the back of the neck. The leather will gradually soften and change in tone with exposure to movement, moisture, body heat, and repeated wear.

Natural differences in grain, color, and surface texture may be visible in the leather. These characteristics are inherent to the material rather than defects.

Modified Vintage Work-Jacket Design
The jacket incorporates recognizable elements of early work-jacket construction, including a short body, low collar, vertical front pleats, riveted patch pockets, set-in sleeves, cuff slits, rear action pleats, a center-seamed back, and an adjustable cinch-back.

Rather than serving as a direct reproduction of one specific historical garment, this model combines these traditional construction details with Studio D'Artisan's proprietary GL-3 denim specification and the natural coloration of Amami Dorozome mud dyeing.

The result is a modified work-jacket design that retains the practical structure of vintage clothing while presenting a distinctive brown color and fabric texture developed through specialized Japanese weaving and dyeing processes.

Natural-Dye Color Transfer
This garment is colored with natural dye, and excess pigment remaining on or near the surface may transfer through friction. Until the initial excess color has gradually been reduced through wear and washing, the jacket should be kept away from light-colored clothing, bags, upholstery, footwear, and other items that may easily absorb pigment.

Color transfer may occur when the jacket is dry, but the risk increases when the fabric is damp from rain, perspiration, washing, or high humidity. Friction at the cuffs, underarms, waistband, collar, and areas that contact bags or seats may also cause pigment to transfer.

Do not place the wet or damp garment directly against other clothing or household surfaces. Do not leave the jacket soaking in water or folded while wet, as dissolved dye may migrate and create uneven staining.

Washing and Care Precautions
Wash this jacket separately from other garments. Use cold water and a mild detergent. Do not use chlorine bleach, oxygen bleach, hot water, or a tumble dryer.

After washing, remove the jacket promptly, reshape it carefully, and allow it to air-dry in the shade. Avoid leaving the garment wet for an extended period. Prolonged soaking or contact with other wet materials may cause dye to bleed or transfer.

Because of the natural dyeing process, some color loss is expected during washing. Variations in fading and surface color are part of the intended character of the garment.

Made in Japan
The jacket is made in Japan using Studio D'Artisan's original 15 oz. GL-3 loom-woven cotton denim and finished with traditional Amami Dorozome mud dyeing. Its fabric, construction, hardware, and functional details combine Japanese textile production with the practical design principles of classic workwear.


Toyoda GL-3 Power Loom

An Early Japanese Power Loom
The GL-3 is an early Japanese shuttle-type power loom manufactured by Toyoda Automatic Loom Works, now known as Toyota Industries Corporation. It was developed before the widespread adoption of modern high-speed textile machinery and reflects an earlier stage of Japanese weaving technology.

Only a limited number of GL-3 looms remain in operation today. Their rarity, low production capacity, and distinctive weaving characteristics have made them highly valued for producing specialized fabrics with pronounced surface variation.

Difficult to Maintain
Replacement parts for the GL-3 are no longer commercially manufactured. When a component becomes worn or damaged, usable parts may need to be recovered from another retired or non-operational GL-3 loom.

Keeping the machine in working condition requires experienced technicians who understand its mechanical timing, shuttle movement, yarn tension, take-up system, and other operating characteristics.

Small changes in alignment or mechanical adjustment can affect both the stability of the weaving process and the appearance of the finished fabric. Regular inspection, careful adjustment, and continued maintenance are therefore essential.

Extremely Slow Weaving Speed
A GL-3 can weave only approximately five meters of fabric per hour. This is considerably slower than contemporary high-speed looms designed for large-scale industrial production.

From a manufacturing perspective, the GL-3 is highly inefficient. It requires more time, closer supervision, and greater mechanical attention to produce a relatively small quantity of fabric.

However, the slow operating speed allows the yarns to be woven without creating the highly compressed, smooth, and mechanically uniform surface commonly associated with modern mass-produced textiles.

Why the GL-3 Is Called a "Phantom Loom"
The GL-3 is sometimes referred to as a "phantom loom" because very few operational machines remain, replacement parts are difficult to obtain, and the technical knowledge required to maintain them is increasingly specialized.

The term also refers to the distinctive fabric character produced by the machine. Depending on the yarn and weaving specification, the GL-3 can produce visible neps, slubs, uneven elevations, and subtle variations in surface density that are difficult to reproduce with modern high-speed equipment.

These characteristics are not manufacturing defects. They result from the combination of irregular yarns, low-speed weaving, carefully controlled tension, and the mechanical properties of the older loom.

Fabric Characteristics Produced by the GL-3
Fabric woven on the GL-3 typically has a substantial hand and a visibly irregular surface. Differences in yarn thickness, tension, and placement create raised and recessed areas throughout the cloth.

Small neps, slubs, loose surface fibers, and variations in texture may be visible. Neps are small groups of entangled fibers, while slubs are thicker sections formed within intentionally irregular yarns.

Rather than appearing perfectly flat and uniform, the surface contains subtle variations that become more noticeable under changing light and through continued use.

The exact appearance and hand of the fabric depend on the yarn count, yarn irregularity, warp density, weft density, weaving tension, and other production specifications selected for each fabric.

Craftsmanship Rather Than Production Efficiency
Producing fabric on the GL-3 requires substantially more time and manual involvement than weaving on modern industrial machinery.

The loom must be carefully maintained, weaving conditions must be monitored, and mechanical adjustments may be required during production. The objective is not maximum output or complete visual uniformity, but the creation of fabric with controlled irregularity and distinctive surface character.

Each length of fabric reflects the interaction between the loom, the yarn specification, the mechanical settings, and the judgment of the loom operator.

The GL-3 therefore represents a production method that prioritizes fabric character, technical skill, and careful small-scale manufacturing over speed and efficiency.

Handling Amami Dorozome Mud-Dyed Products

Traditional Amami Dorozome Dyeing
Amami Dorozome is a traditional mud-dyeing method practiced on Amami Oshima in southern Japan.

The process uses a botanical dye extracted from the Techi tree, also known in Japanese as Sharinbai. The wood and bark contain natural tannins that can bond with textile fibers and react with iron.

The material is repeatedly immersed in the plant-based dye solution so that the tannins penetrate the fibers. It is then treated with iron-rich mud from Amami Oshima.

The iron in the mud reacts with the tannins and gradually deepens and fixes the color. Multiple dyeing and mud-treatment cycles are required to build the characteristic earthy tone.

Natural Color Variation
Amami Dorozome does not produce the mechanically uniform appearance associated with conventional synthetic dyeing.

Minor differences in color depth, concentration, and surface tone may occur between individual products. Subtle variations may also be visible within different areas of the same product.

Seams, folds, reinforced areas, and sections containing multiple layers of fabric may absorb or retain the dye differently from single-layer areas.

These variations are inherent characteristics of the traditional dyeing process and should not be regarded as defects.

Color Transfer Through Friction
Natural dye remaining on or near the surface may transfer to other materials through friction.

Particular care should be taken when a mud-dyed product comes into contact with white or light-colored clothing, bags, shoes, furniture, automobile seats, upholstery, or other finished surfaces.

Areas exposed to repeated rubbing may release color more readily. Color transfer is often more noticeable during the early period of use, although it may continue depending on moisture, friction, and washing conditions.

Color Transfer When Wet or Damp
Moisture can increase the possibility of dye transfer. Perspiration, rain, washing water, humidity, or other sources of moisture may cause the surface dye to become more mobile.

When the product is damp, avoid direct contact with light-colored clothing, bags, furniture, car seats, and other materials that may absorb the dye.

Do not leave the wet product folded, compressed, or placed against another item for an extended period. Prolonged contact while wet may result in color transfer, uneven staining, or migration of dye between different sections.

Washing Instructions
Wash mud-dyed products separately from other items because released dye may transfer during washing.

When appropriate for the product, turn it inside out before washing. This reduces direct abrasion against the dyed outer surface and may help limit unnecessary surface color loss.

Use cold or lukewarm water, a mild detergent, and a gentle washing method. Avoid excessive mechanical agitation, scrubbing, brushing, or concentrated rubbing.

Do not use chlorine bleach or oxygen bleach. Avoid hot water and tumble drying unless specifically permitted by the care label attached to the product.

After washing, remove the product promptly, reshape it carefully, and allow it to air-dry naturally in the shade. Do not leave it soaking or wet for an extended period.

Always follow the specific care instructions provided on the product label.

Drying and Sunlight Precautions
When appropriate, turn the product inside out before drying and place it in a well-ventilated shaded area.

Avoid prolonged exposure to direct sunlight. Strong ultraviolet light may cause natural dyes to fade, discolor, or change unevenly, particularly when the product remains exposed in the same position for an extended period.

Direct sunlight should not be used intentionally to darken or develop the color, as it may instead cause unwanted or uneven fading.

Natural Aging and Color Development
The color and surface appearance of Amami Dorozome products will gradually change through use, friction, washing, moisture, and exposure to air.

Areas that receive frequent contact may become lighter, while recessed or less exposed areas may retain a darker tone. The resulting appearance will vary according to how the product is used, cleaned, dried, and stored.

No two naturally dyed products will develop in exactly the same manner.

Characteristics of Natural Dye
Color fading, surface variation, and occasional color transfer are inherent characteristics of Amami Dorozome and other natural dyeing methods.

These properties differ from the high degree of color uniformity and colorfastness commonly associated with modern synthetic dyes.

Careful handling can reduce unwanted transfer and uneven fading, but it cannot completely prevent the natural color from changing over time.

Please handle Amami Dorozome products with appropriate care and enjoy the individual color development and surface character created through continued use.
Care Instructions
Machine wash on a gentle cycle at a maximum water temperature of 40°C (104°F).
Do not use chlorine bleach or oxygen bleach.
Iron at a medium temperature with a pressing cloth placed between the iron and the garment.
Do not dry clean.
Due to the nature of the dye, color loss may occur. Wash separately from other garments.
Due to the characteristics of the fabric, slight shrinkage may occur after washing.
Color may transfer to other clothing, accessories, upholstery, or other surfaces through friction or when the garment is damp from perspiration, rain, or other moisture.
